sections.title: Lesson 6.1: Nonqualified Accounts
sections.overview: Nonqualified accounts are non-retirement accounts that may or may not be tax-deferred. This lesson covers individual, joint, business, trust, custodial, and education accounts, along with key account features such as TOD designations and powers of attorney. Mastery of ownership transfer rules at death and the documentation required for each account type is essential.
key_concepts: Individual account: one beneficial owner; assets pass through estate at death unless TOD added.
Joint account: two or more adult co-owners; all signatures required to open; checks payable to all registered names and endorsed by all; mail to single address acceptable.
JTWROS (Joint Tenants with Right of Survivorship): undivided equal interest; deceased tenant's share passes to surviving tenant(s); common for spouses.

TIC (Tenants in Common): each tenant owns a specified fractional interest; deceased tenant's portion goes to that tenant's estate (account frozen until estate paperwork processed); assumed equal if no agreement.
TOD (Transfer on Death): bypasses probate but NOT estate tax; available on individual and JTWROS accounts; on joint accounts, TOD activates only after the last surviving tenant dies.
Power of Attorney (POA): written authorization for a non-owner to access an account; granted to a person, not a firm; carries fiduciary duty; all POAs terminate upon death of either party.
Full POA (FPOA): may deposit, withdraw, and trade; rarely approved for an RR over a non-family account.
Limited POA (LPOA): trading authority only — no withdrawals (also called limited trading authorization).
Durable POA: survives the grantor's incapacity but still terminates at death.
Sole Proprietor / d/b/a accounts: owned by individual; checks may be payable to owner or business name.
Partnership account: requires written partnership agreement and authorization naming who may trade; amended annually if changes occur; partnership agreement must permit margin if desired.

Corporate account: requires copy of the corporate charter (proof of existence) AND corporate resolution (authorizes account and designates persons who may trade); charter must permit margin if desired.
Trust roles: Grantor/Settlor (creates and funds), Trustee (manages), Beneficiary (benefits).
Living trust: created and funded during grantor's lifetime; Decedent's trust: funded via will/estate after death.
Revocable trust: grantor may modify or revoke; assets remain in grantor's estate; grantor is often also trustee and beneficiary.
Irrevocable trust: cannot be modified; grantor relinquishes control; assets may be removed from estate (grantor cannot also serve as trustee or beneficiary for estate-tax exclusion).
Custodial accounts (UGMA/UTMA): one custodian, one minor beneficiary; minor's SSN used; income taxed at minor's rate; opened only as CASH accounts.
UTMA: allows real estate; assets held in custodial name until age 21–25 depending on state.
UGMA: no real estate; assets pass to minor at age of majority (now offered in only one state).

Custodial restrictions: no margin, no naked options, no short sales, no speculative investments; covered call writing permitted; cash proceeds and dividends must be reinvested within a reasonable time; rights/warrants must be exercised or sold.
Custodian may be reimbursed for expenses; donor-custodian may NOT be compensated, only reimbursed.
Coverdell ESA: $2,000/year max per beneficiary until age 18; after-tax contributions; tax-free qualified withdrawals for K–12 and college; account must be depleted or rolled by age 30.
Fiduciary accounts: include trustees, executors, administrators, guardians, custodians, receivers, conservators; subject to prudent investor rule; margin only if expressly authorized in documents.
Numbered accounts: permitted only with written acknowledgment of ownership on file; used for privacy.
rules: JTWROS — all tenants own an undivided equal interest; survivor takes all.
TIC — each tenant must specify a percentage of interest; decedent's share to estate.
TOD — avoids probate but not estate tax; available on individual and JTWROS only.
All POAs end upon death of either party, including durable POAs.

Corporate margin requires corporate charter to NOT prohibit margin; partnership margin requires partnership agreement to NOT prohibit margin; trust margin requires the trust document to SPECIFICALLY ALLOW margin.
Custodial accounts are cash accounts only — no margin, no pledging as collateral.
Coverdell nonqualified distributions: ordinary income tax plus 10% penalty on earnings.
Fiduciary may not share in account profits but may charge reasonable fees.
mnemonics: JTWROS = 'Joint Together With Right Of Survivorship' — survivor takes all (Undivided interest).
TIC = 'To-the-Individual's-estate Coverage' — fractional interest goes to estate.
POA dies when either Person dies (Owner or Attorney).
Trust margin permission rule: 'Trust must SAY YES' (silence = no); Partnership/Corporate rule: 'must not SAY NO' (silence = yes).

sections.title: Lesson 6.2: Qualified Accounts
sections.overview: Qualified accounts are retirement vehicles that offer tax-deferred growth and are governed by IRS contribution, distribution, and RMD rules. This lesson covers Traditional and Roth IRAs as well as employer-sponsored defined benefit and defined contribution plans. Note that under SECURE 2.0, the RMD beginning age is now 73 (rising to 75 in 2033) and the RMD shortfall penalty is now 25% (10% if timely corrected).
key_concepts: IRAs technically are not 'qualified' plans (no employer sponsor) but follow similar contribution and distribution rules.
Contributions must come from EARNED INCOME (salary, wages, tips, self-employment) — not from dividends, interest, or capital gains.
No age limit for contributing to either Traditional or Roth IRA (SECURE Act).
Catch-up contribution for age 50+: indexed in $100 increments under SECURE 2.0 (e.g., $1,100 for tax year 2026); the specific dollar limit is generally not tested.
Traditional IRA: contributions may be tax-deductible (deductibility phases out with AGI if covered by another qualified plan); growth tax-deferred; distributions taxed as ordinary income.
Roth IRA: contributions NOT deductible (after-tax); growth tax-deferred; qualified distributions are tax-free; contribution eligibility phases out at higher AGI.
Roth and Traditional share a combined annual contribution limit across all IRAs owned.
Permissible IRA investments: stocks, bonds, mutual funds, UITs, government securities, U.S.-minted gold/silver coins, annuities.
Prohibited IRA investments: collectibles, life insurance, antiques, gems, rare coins, stamps, artwork.
Inappropriate IRA practices: short sales, speculative options, margin trading, municipal securities (tax-exempt status wasted); covered calls permitted.
Rollover: customer takes possession of funds; must redeposit within 60 calendar days; one rollover per rolling 12-month period (per person across all IRAs).
Transfer (custodian-to-custodian / direct rollover): unlimited; assets move directly between custodians.

Pre-59½ withdrawal: 10% penalty + ordinary income tax. Exceptions to penalty: death, disability, first-time home purchase (up to $10,000), qualified education expenses, medical insurance for unemployed, medical expenses exceeding AGI threshold.
RMD beginning age: 73 (under SECURE 2.0, for those reaching 72 after 12/31/2022); rises to 75 for those reaching 74 after 12/31/2032.
First RMD may be delayed until April 1 of the year following the year the owner reaches the RMD age — but a second RMD will be required by December 31 of that same year.
RMD shortfall penalty: 25% of the shortfall (reduced from 50% by SECURE 2.0); further reduced to 10% if corrected within the IRS correction window.
RMDs across multiple Traditional IRAs may be aggregated and taken from any one or combination of accounts.
Roth IRA qualified distribution requirements: account held 5+ years AND owner is age 59½+, deceased, disabled, or first-time homebuyer (up to $10,000).
Roth IRAs have NO RMDs during the owner's lifetime.
Excess IRA contributions: 6% penalty per year on the excess until withdrawn.
Defined Benefit Plan (pension): formula-based benefit at retirement (typically based on years of service, age, salary); employer bears investment risk; uses actuary to determine funding.
Defined Contribution Plan: contributions defined; benefit varies with investment performance; employee bears investment risk; assets portable.
Examples of defined contribution plans: 401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing, money purchase, SIMPLE plans.
Private pension payments are fixed (purchasing-power risk); government pensions often have COLA.
rules: IRA contributions require earned income.
Rollovers: 60 calendar days; one per rolling 12-month period per person.
Pre-59½ distributions: 10% penalty unless exception applies.
RMDs begin at age 73 (SECURE 2.0); shortfall penalty 25% (10% if timely corrected).
Roth qualified distribution: 5-year holding period AND a triggering event (59½, death, disability, first home).
Excess contribution penalty: 6% per year until removed.
Life insurance and collectibles prohibited in IRAs.
formulas: Defined Benefit Example: Annual Benefit = Years of Service × Benefit Percentage × Final Average Salary (capped at plan maximum)
RMD = Prior Year-End Account Balance / IRS Life Expectancy Factor
mnemonics: Roth Qualified = '5 + 1' — 5-year holding PLUS one triggering event (59½, death, disability, first-home $10K).
IRA prohibited: 'CLAMS' — Collectibles, Life insurance, Antiques, Margin/Munis, Speculation.
DB = 'Defined Benefit, Boss's Burden' (employer bears risk); DC = 'Defined Contribution, Customer's Concern' (employee bears risk).
Rollover rule: '60-1-1' — 60 days, 1 per year, 1 per person.

sections.title: Lesson 6.3: Account Features
sections.overview: This lesson covers the operational features of brokerage accounts: cash vs. margin vs. fee-based structures, the documentation and regulatory requirements for margin trading, and the rules governing solicited, unsolicited, and discretionary trades. Margin allows leverage but requires specific agreements and is governed jointly by Federal Reserve Regulation T and FINRA Rule 4210.
key_concepts: Cash account: full payment required by settlement date; payment under Regulation T no later than 2 business days after standard settlement (T+1 settlement → payment by T+3 under Reg T).
Accounts that MUST be cash: IRAs/retirement plans, UGMA/UTMA custodial accounts.
Long margin: customer borrows cash from BD to purchase securities; pays interest until loan repaid.
Short margin: customer borrows stock to sell short, profiting if price declines; all short sales executed in a margin account.
Leverage in margin magnifies both gains and losses (Reg T 50% effectively doubles return percentage on price movement).
Hypothecation: customer pledges securities to BD as collateral for margin loan.
Rehypothecation: BD repledges customer securities to a bank as collateral under Reg U.
Customer securities may be commingled with other customers' securities for hypothecation (with permission) but NEVER commingled with firm-owned securities.

Margin account forms: Credit Agreement (mandatory — discloses loan terms and interest), Hypothecation Agreement (mandatory — pledges securities), Consent to Loan Agreement (OPTIONAL — allows firm to lend customer securities to other parties for short sales).
Risk disclosure document required at account opening and annually thereafter.
Margin risks: customer can lose more than initial deposit; firm may liquidate without customer choosing which securities; no entitlement to extension; in-house margin can be raised without notice.
Marginable securities: exchange-listed stocks/bonds, Nasdaq stocks, FRB-approved OTC issues, warrants.
Non-marginable: options, rights, non-NMS OTC issues, insurance contracts.
Mutual funds and new issues: not marginable for purchase, but usable as collateral after 30 days of ownership.
Exempt from Reg T: U.S. Treasuries, agency issues, municipal securities (BD sets own requirements but must meet FINRA maintenance).
Initial margin deposit: greater of Reg T (50%) OR FINRA minimum ($2,000, or 100% if purchase is under $2,000).
FINRA maintenance: 25% of long market value; 30% of short market value.
Maintenance call: issued when equity drops below maintenance requirement; failure to deposit allows firm to liquidate positions.
House call: firm's stricter in-house maintenance requirement above FINRA's minimum.
Margin vs. Marginable: Margin = required equity deposit; Marginable = security eligible to serve as collateral.
Fee-based account: flat or asset-based periodic fee covers all trading; appropriate for active traders; inappropriate for buy-and-hold investors.
Solicited trade: prompted by BD or RR recommendation; must be marked 'solicited' on ticket.
Unsolicited trade: customer initiates without prompting; marked 'unsolicited.'
Discretionary trade: RR chooses one or more of the three As (Action, Amount, Asset) without customer's specific direction.
Time and price discretion is NOT considered discretion (customer may grant this freely without written authority).
Discretionary authority requires: written customer authorization PRIOR to first discretionary trade; written principal approval; principal review of each discretionary trade promptly after entry.
Discretion belongs to the representative — terminates if RR leaves the firm or dies.

Wrap account: single fee covers asset allocation, management, execution, and administration; generally an investment advisory account requiring Investment Advisers Act of 1940 registration; must disclose that components may be obtained separately for less.
rules: Regulation T (FRB): 50% initial margin requirement; payment due T+1 settlement + 2 business days = T+3.
Regulation U (FRB): governs bank loans to BDs secured by customer securities.
FINRA Rule 4210: initial minimum equity $2,000; maintenance 25% long / 30% short.
Pattern Day Trader (FINRA 4210): 4+ day trades within 5 business days requires $25,000 minimum equity.
Credit and Hypothecation agreements are MANDATORY; Consent to Loan agreement is OPTIONAL (regulatorily — firm may make it mandatory by policy).
Discretionary accounts require prior written authorization and principal approval (FINRA Rule 3260).
Solicited/unsolicited marking is required on every order ticket; mismarking is a violation.
formulas: Required Initial Deposit = greater of (Reg T × Purchase Price) OR FINRA Minimum ($2,000 or 100% of purchase if under $2,000)
Long Maintenance Equity = Market Value × 25% (FINRA minimum)
Short Maintenance Equity = Market Value × 30% (FINRA minimum)
Margin Return % = (Gain or Loss) / Initial Equity Deposit
mnemonics: Three As of Discretion: Action, Amount, Asset (Buy/Sell, How Much, What). Time and Price are NOT discretion.
Margin forms: 'CHL' — Credit (mandatory), Hypothecation (mandatory), Loan consent (optional).
Reg T vs. Reg U: T = Trader (BD to customer); U = Underlying bank loan (Bank to BD).
Marginable rights/options test: 'RIO is OUT' — Rights, Insurance, Options are NOT marginable.
